Getting started with NICHESv2

Source: vignettes/NICHESv2.Rmd
NICHESv2.Rmd

NICHESv2 scores ligand-receptor (LR) signaling between individual pairs of cells. For each directed cell pair and each LR pair, it asks whether the sending cell expresses the ligand and the receiving cell expresses the receptor. It keeps every non-zero score, so you can trace a signal back to the exact cells that produced it.

This vignette runs the whole workflow on a small synthetic dataset that ships with the package, so every step takes a moment and needs no download.

library(NICHESv2)
library(data.table)

Inputs

create_NICHESObject() needs three things: a gene-by-cell expression matrix, cell metadata, and an LR database. The bundled NICHESv2_inputs list holds all three, for 50 genes and 80 cells.

data(NICHESv2_inputs)
names(NICHESv2_inputs)
#> [1] "count.mtx" "meta.data" "LRM.db"

dim(NICHESv2_inputs$count.mtx)
#> [1] 50 80
head(NICHESv2_inputs$meta.data, 3)
x y nCount_RNA celltype
Cell_1 0.136 0.298 66 TypeA
Cell_2 0.238 0.172 53 TypeA
Cell_3 0.225 0.240 55 TypeA 
head(NICHESv2_inputs$LRM.db, 3)
ligand receptor pathway
Gene1 Gene2 PathwayA
Gene3 Gene4 PathwayB
Gene5 Gene6 PathwayC

The column names of the matrix must match the row names of the metadata. Spatial mode needs x and y columns in the metadata.

Build a NICHESObject

Here each cell is connected to its spatial neighbors using k = 5. Only mutual nearest neighbors become edges, and every cell also gets a self-loop for autocrine signaling.

obj <- create_NICHESObject(
  count.mtx = NICHESv2_inputs$count.mtx,
  meta.data = NICHESv2_inputs$meta.data,
  LRM.db    = NICHESv2_inputs$LRM.db,
  mode      = "spatial",
  k         = 5L,
  method    = "product",
  verbose   = FALSE
)
dim(obj)
#> cells genes edges  LRMs 
#>    80    50   354    15

An edge is one directed cell pair. method = "product" multiplies the sender’s ligand expression by the receiver’s receptor expression, and "minimum" takes the smaller of the two. To use a fixed radius instead of k, pass rad; Explore_Radius_Neighborhood() helps you choose a value.

For larger datasets, set n.cores to score LR pairs in parallel. This uses socket clusters, so it works on every platform.

Inside the object

A NICHESObject is a list with 15 slots, which you read with $.

Level Slots
Cell $cell.list, $cell.data, $cell.meta
Edge $edge.list, $edge.data, $edge.meta
Neighborhood $neighborhood.cell.list, $neighborhood.edge.list, $neighborhood.meta
Gene and LRM $gene.list, $gene.meta, $LRM.list, $LRM.meta
Extras $segmentation, $aggregations

Scores are stored in long format, with one row for each non-zero (edge, LRM) pair. This keeps memory use tied to how much signal exists, not to the number of possible combinations.

head(obj$edge.data, 3)
edge LRM score score.norm
Cell_10|Cell_1 Gene9|Gene10 21 1
Cell_10|Cell_10 Gene15|Gene16 35 1
Cell_10|Cell_4 Gene9|Gene10 18 1

Edge IDs have the form "SendingCell|ReceivingCell" and LRM IDs have the form "ligand|receptor". $edge.data is a data.table, so you can summarize it directly. These are the strongest LR pairs overall:

obj$edge.data[, .(total.score = sum(score)), by = LRM][order(-total.score)][1:3]
LRM total.score
Gene27|Gene28_Gene29 632
Gene29_Gene30|Gene28_Gene30 600
Gene25_Gene26|Gene27 574

$edge.meta carries each cell’s metadata onto its edges, with Sending. and Receiving. prefixes, which makes it easy to filter by cell type:

obj$edge.meta[, .(edges = .N), by = .(Sending.celltype, Receiving.celltype)][1:3]
Sending.celltype Receiving.celltype edges
TypeA TypeA 132
TypeB TypeB 115
TypeB TypeC 2

Aggregate by neighborhood

Each cell’s neighborhood is filled in when the object is built. aggregate_NICHESObject() summarizes each one per LRM, and with cell.type.col it also reports which cell types surround each cell.

obj <- aggregate_NICHESObject(obj, cell.type.col = "celltype", verbose = FALSE)
names(obj$aggregations)
#> [1] "neighborhood.edge.agg"    "neighborhood.composition"

$aggregations$neighborhood.edge.agg has one row per (cell, LRM). It sorts each neighborhood edge into five categories relative to the focal cell: in, out, cross (between two neighbors), self.autocrine and other.autocrine.

agg <- obj$aggregations$neighborhood.edge.agg
agg[, .(cell, LRM, score.in.sum, score.out.sum, score.cross.sum)][1:3]
cell LRM score.in.sum score.out.sum score.cross.sum
Cell_1 Gene11|Gene12 10 0 0
Cell_1 Gene13|Gene14 0 0 8
Cell_1 Gene15|Gene16 0 0 0

$aggregations$neighborhood.composition has one row per cell:

comp <- obj$aggregations$neighborhood.composition
comp[, .(cell, TypeA.neighbor.prop, TypeB.neighbor.prop, TypeC.neighbor.prop)][1:3]
cell TypeA.neighbor.prop TypeB.neighbor.prop TypeC.neighbor.prop
Cell_1 1 0 0
Cell_10 1 0 0
Cell_11 1 0 0

Subset to cells of interest

Aggregate first, then subset. Each retained cell keeps its neighborhood entries and aggregation rows unchanged, so its values still describe its whole neighborhood in the full tissue, including neighbors you didn’t keep.

type.a <- obj$cell.meta[celltype == "TypeA", cell]
sub <- obj[type.a]
dim(sub)
#> cells genes edges  LRMs 
#>    30    50   132    15

identical(
  sub$aggregations$neighborhood.edge.agg[, score.in.sum],
  agg[cell %in% type.a, score.in.sum]
)
#> [1] TRUE

The edge slots of a subset hold only edges between retained cells. Summing a cell’s rows in sub$edge.data can therefore give less than its aggregation row.

Because those removed edges are gone, aggregations can’t be recomputed on the subset, and trying stops with an error. To analyze the subset as a separate tissue, rebuild its neighborhoods first:

separate <- add_neighborhoods(sub, overwrite = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
separate <- aggregate_NICHESObject(separate, verbose = FALSE)

Data without coordinates

For scRNA-seq data, mode = "nonspatial" pairs cells by random sampling within each pair of cell types. It needs cell.type.col, and seed makes the sampling repeatable.

ns <- create_NICHESObject(
  count.mtx     = NICHESv2_inputs$count.mtx,
  meta.data     = NICHESv2_inputs$meta.data,
  LRM.db        = NICHESv2_inputs$LRM.db,
  mode          = "nonspatial",
  cell.type.col = "celltype",
  verbose       = FALSE
)
dim(ns)
#> cells genes edges  LRMs 
#>    80    50   230    15

Using your own data

LR databases

Pass a database name to LRM.db, and set species to match your data.

db <- load_LRM_database("connectomedb2025", species = "human", verbose = FALSE)
nrow(db)
#> [1] 3550

"connectomedb2025" (the default in load_LRM_database()) and "fantom5" are bundled for human, mouse, rat and pig. "omnipath" needs internet access and the OmnipathR package, and covers human, mouse and rat. You can also pass your own data frame. Multi-gene complexes are written with underscores, such as "COL1A1_COL1A2".

Seurat objects

extract_NICHESInputs_Seurat() works with Seurat V4 and V5 objects, so you don’t need to update an older object first. It returns count.mtx and meta.data, ready for create_NICHESObject(). For spatial data, add the coordinates to meta.data yourself as x and y columns; SeuratObject::GetTissueCoordinates() returns them.

seu <- SeuratObject::CreateSeuratObject(
  counts    = NICHESv2_inputs$count.mtx,
  meta.data = NICHESv2_inputs$meta.data
)
inputs <- extract_NICHESInputs_Seurat(seu, layer = "counts", verbose = FALSE)
dim(inputs$count.mtx)
#> [1] 50 80

The layer you choose sets what the scores mean: raw counts give absolute magnitudes, and normalized expression gives relative scores.

AnnData files

extract_NICHESInputs_AnnData() reads .h5ad files with rhdf5, so it doesn’t need Python.

h5ad <- system.file("extdata", "NICHESv2_example.h5ad", package = "NICHESv2")
inputs <- extract_NICHESInputs_AnnData(h5ad, verbose = FALSE)
dim(inputs$count.mtx)
#> [1] 50 80

Exporting to TissuePlex

export_to_TissuePlex() writes one Parquet file of edges and needs the arrow package. To view the file in tissue coordinates, see the TissuePlex manual.

out.file <- tempfile(fileext = ".parquet")
export_to_TissuePlex(obj, output.path = out.file)
unlink(out.file)

Where to go next

See ?create_NICHESObject for every construction option, ?add_neighborhood_edge_agg for all 27 aggregation columns, and ?"[.NICHESObject" for the subsetting rules. ?NICHESv2 gives an overview.

The website has tutorials on public spatial and non-spatial datasets.
